issues.legal_issue: A review petition may be allowed to correct a clear error in an earlier judgment.
material_facts: The earlier judgment inaccurately described the Board as an institution dating from 1949 and as composed of the seniormost members of the family branches.
The Court found that the Board had instead been constituted under an earlier royal proclamation and that seniormost membership was not required.
issues.conclusion: The review petition was allowed in substantial part, including to correct the inaccurate description of the Board and clarify the earlier judgment.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that when a clear error in its judgment is revealed, it may review and correct the judgment in order to be ultimately right. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this proposition.

predicates.review_proceeding: A party asks the court to review an earlier judgment.
predicates.clear_error_in_earlier_judgment_shown: The reviewing court finds a clear error in the earlier judgment.

issues.definition: When a review proceeding shows a clear error in an earlier judgment, the earlier judgment is corrected on review.

issues.legal_issue: A family property administration board is validly constituted when its appointments provide fair representation, so far as possible, for each of the relevant family branches, even if its members are not the seniormost members.
material_facts: The Board consisted of trustees nominated by the family ruler under the governing proclamation.
The proclamation required representation, so far as possible, for each of the four main family branches, but did not require selection of the seniormost members.
The Board had functioned for decades, and its composition was challenged on the ground that its members were not the seniormost members of the branches.
issues.conclusion: The Board was validly constituted; fair representation of the branches, so far as possible, was required, but seniormost membership was not.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied sections 2(a) and 4 of the 1124 Proclamation: the Board was made up of nominated trustees, and its composition had to secure representation, so far as possible, for each of the four main family branches. The ruler could choose seniormost members but was not required to do so.

predicates.family_property_board: A board is responsible for administering or partitioning the property of a family.
predicates.trustees_nominated_by_family_ruler: The family ruler nominated the trustees who made up the board.
predicates.fair_representation_of_each_branch_possi: The board's composition provided fair representation, so far as possible, for each main branch of the family.

issues.definition: A family property board whose trustees were nominated by the family ruler and whose composition fairly represents each branch, so far as possible, is validly composed without having to select the seniormost members.

issues.legal_issue: Work already undertaken by a family property board in a partition may stand, but decisions affecting sharers who lacked an opportunity to participate must be reconsidered through a fair process.
material_facts: The Board had carried out valuations, effected sales and made provisional allotments while working toward partition.
Competent valuers and engineers had assisted the Board, and family members had participated through an advisory committee.
Some sharers had not had a say in valuations and sales, and the Court considered that objections and hearings were necessary.
issues.conclusion: The Board's existing work was not to be discarded, but valuations, sales and provisional allotments could stand only subject to a process allowing objections, consideration on their merits and a hearing for parties affected by the Board's decisions.
issues.legal_principle: The Board's decisions had to be reasonable and fair and comply with natural justice. The Court required the draft partition materials to be available for inspection, objections to be considered on their merits, and affected parties to receive a brief hearing. No earlier case was relied on for these directions.

predicates.family_partition_proceeding: A board is carrying out a partition of family property.
predicates.board_has_completed_substantial_partitio: The board has already undertaken substantial work on valuations, sales or provisional allotments.
predicates.affected_sharers_lacked_opportunity_to_o: One or more sharers affected by the board's work had not had an opportunity to raise objections.

issues.definition: In a family partition where substantial board work is complete but affected sharers lacked an opportunity to object, that work remains subject to fair consideration of objections and a hearing.

issues.legal_issue: Group allotments in a family partition are permissible only when the sharers assigned to each group consent; otherwise, each member is entitled to an individual per capita share.
material_facts: The Board had made group allotments as part of the partition process.
The Court held that group allotments could be justified by practical considerations and acceptance by the members concerned, but that individual members were otherwise entitled to per capita shares.
issues.conclusion: Group allotments were permissible if the sharers in the group consented; without their consent, each member was entitled to a per capita share.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the equal-share rule in section 4 of the 1976 Act and held that group allotment could be used only with the consent of the sharers concerned, supported by practical considerations. Otherwise, each member was entitled to a per capita share.

predicates.family_partition_proceeding: A board is carrying out a partition of family property.
predicates.group_allotment_proposed: The board proposes to allot property jointly to a group of sharers rather than individually.

issues.definition: When a group allotment is proposed in a family partition, the allotment requires the consent of the group members; without it, individual per capita shares apply.

issues.legal_issue: For the royal family's division in status and determination of share entitlements, the applicable date was the commencement of the general law abolishing the joint family system, while the surviving special legislation continued to govern how the property was partitioned.
material_facts: The family remained joint because the family ruler had not made the declaration required under the earlier special partition law.
The general law abolishing the joint family system came into force while the family remained joint and applied, in the majority's view, to the family.
The special proclamation and partition law were omitted from the general law's repeal schedule, and the later amending law preserved the Board's role and prior partition work.
The justices agreed on the result concerning the date and partition, although Justice Koshal disagreed with the majority's reasoning about the general law's initial application.
issues.conclusion: The majority held that the family was divided in status when the general law came into force, with shares determined at that point, including the share of a child in the womb; the Board was to work out the partition by metes and bounds. Justice Koshal concurred in the result but considered that the estate remained impartible under the earlier special law until the later amendment made the general law's share rules specifically applicable.
issues.legal_principle: The majority relied on section 4(2) of the 1976 Act, which deemed members of covered joint families to hold property as tenants in common as if a per capita partition had occurred; section 7 and its schedule, which left the proclamation and the 1961 Act unrepealed; section 4 of the 1961 Act concerning shares, including a child in the womb; and sections 8 and 9 of the 1978 Act, which preserved the special regime and acts already done. Justice Koshal relied on section 3 of the 1961 Act and the 1978 amendments to conclude that the general law's share rule applied to the family and fixed entitlement by reference to the general law's commencement.

predicates.family_remained_joint_when_general_aboli: The family had not already become divided under the special partition procedure when the general family-law change took effect.
predicates.general_abolition_law_applied_to_family: The court determined that the general change in family law applied to the family for fixing division in status and share entitlements.
predicates.special_partition_law_survived: The special family-property legislation remained in force rather than being repealed by the general law.

issues.definition: When a family remained joint at the commencement of a general family-law change that applied to it, and its special partition law survived, share entitlements were fixed at that commencement.

issues.legal_issue: The board designated by surviving special legislation, rather than a civil court, has authority to carry out the partition of the family estate by metes and bounds.
material_facts: The special partition legislation assigned the partition process to the Board.
The general law's repeal schedule did not repeal that special legislation.
The later amending law confirmed that the proclamation and special partition legislation continued to apply to the estate and preserved actions already taken under them.
issues.conclusion: The Board alone was to carry out the partition by metes and bounds; the civil court was not to do so.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on section 3 of the 1961 Act, which assigned partition to the Board, read with section 7 and the schedule of the 1976 Act, which did not repeal the special legislation, and sections 8 and 9 of the 1978 Act, which continued that regime and preserved prior actions.

predicates.family_estate_partition_proceeding: A proceeding concerns partition of an estate governed by a special family-property regime.
predicates.surviving_special_law_assigns_partition_: A special law that remains in force assigns the partition of the estate to a board.

issues.definition: When a family-estate partition is governed by a surviving special law that assigns partition to a board, the board has exclusive authority to partition the estate by metes and bounds.
